source_refs.note: Book p. 102: 6.6 Geometric Mean, definition G/a = b/G, G = ±sqrt(ab), side Note on n G.M.s between a and b

blocks.text: Pichle hisson mein aap ne arithmetic mean (A.M.) parha tha: do numbers ke beech woh number jo un ke saath mil kar A.P. bana de. Aaj hum usi ka 'bhai' parhenge: geometric mean (G.M.), yani do numbers ke beech woh number jo un ke saath mil kar G.P. (geometric progression, jis mein har term pichli term ko ek hi number se zarb dene se banti hai) bana de. Farq sirf itna hai ke A.P. mein hum jama karte hain aur G.P. mein zarb (multiply).

Kitab ki definition: ek number \(G\) do numbers \(a\) aur \(b\) ke beech geometric mean (G.M.) kehlata hai agar \(a, G, b\) G.P. mein hon. Is liye:
\[\dfrac{G}{a} = \dfrac{b}{G}\]
\[\Rightarrow G^{2} = ab\]
\[\Rightarrow G = \pm\sqrt{ab}\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: \(G_1, G_2, G_3, \ldots, G_n\) ko do numbers \(a\) aur \(b\) ke beech \(n\) G.M.s kaha jata hai agar \(a, G_1, G_2, G_3, \ldots, G_n, b\) G.P. mein hon.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(\frac{G}{a} = \frac{b}{G}\) kyun likha? G.P. ki pehchaan yeh hai ke har term ko us se pehli term par divide karein to hamesha ek hi jawab aata hai; isi ko common ratio \(r\) kehte hain. \(a, G, b\) mein doosri term ko pehli par divide karein to \(\frac{G}{a}\), aur teesri ko doosri par to \(\frac{b}{G}\). Dono \(r\) ke barabar hain, is liye aapas mein bhi barabar. Ab cross-multiply (tirchha zarb) karein to \(G \times G = a \times b\), yani \(G^{2} = ab\).
A.M. se muqabla kijiye: \(a, A, b\) A.P. mein hon to farq barabar hota hai, \(A - a = b - A\), aur \(A = \frac{a+b}{2}\) milta hai. Yaad rakhne ka aasan tareeqa: A.M. 'jama wala darmiyani number' hai, G.M. 'zarb wala darmiyani number'.

blocks.title: Kyun
blocks.text: Aakhir mein \(\pm\) kyun aaya? Kyun ke \(G^{2} = ab\) se \(G\) nikalne ke liye square root lena parta hai, aur har positive number ke do square roots hote hain: ek positive, ek negative. Jaise \(G^{2} = 36\) ho to \(G = 6\) bhi sahi hai aur \(G = -6\) bhi, kyun ke \(6^{2}\) aur \((-6)^{2}\) dono 36 hain.

Chaliye \(4\) aur \(9\) ka G.M. nikaalte hain (yeh hamari misaal hai, kitab ki nahin). Sab se pehle formula yaad kijiye: \(G^{2} = ab\).
\[G^{2} = 4 \times 9 = 36\]
\[G = \pm 6\]
Ab tasdeeq karte hain ke sach mein G.P. banti hai ya nahin. \(4, 6, 9\): \(\frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}\) aur \(\frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}\). Ratio barabar hai, to yeh G.P. hai. Aur \(4, -6, 9\): \(\frac{-6}{4} = -\frac{3}{2}\) aur \(\frac{9}{-6} = -\frac{3}{2}\). Yeh bhi G.P. hai! Isi liye kitab \(\pm\) likhti hai: dono jawab durust hain.
Ghor karein: \(4\) aur \(9\) ka A.M. \(6.5\) hai jab ke positive G.M. \(6\) hai. Yeh farq agle hisse (6.6.1) ka mauzoo hai.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
G.M. ka sign kaise tay ho:
1. Agar \(a\) aur \(b\) dono positive (ya dono negative) hon to \(ab\) positive hai, aur do real G.M.s milte hain: \(\pm\sqrt{ab}\). Sawal mein 'positive G.M.' likha ho to sirf \(+\sqrt{ab}\) lein.
2. Agar ek positive aur doosra negative ho to \(ab\) negative hai, aur negative number ka square root real nahin hota. Misal: \(-1\) aur \(9\) ke beech \(G^{2} = -9\), to \(G = \pm 3i\), kyun ke Unit 1 mein aap ne parha tha ke \(\sqrt{-9} = 3i\). Yani G.M. complex number ban jata hai.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Ab note box wali baat: do numbers ke beech ek nahin, kai G.M.s bhi daale ja sakte hain. Maan lijiye \(a\) aur \(b\) ke beech \(n\) G.M.s daalne hain. To poori G.P. \(a, G_1, \ldots, G_n, b\) ban jati hai, jis mein \(n\) darmiyani terms aur do kinare wali terms hain, yani kul \(n + 2\) terms. Is liye \(b\) is G.P. ki \((n+2)\)th term hai:
\[b = a\,r^{\,n+1}\]
Kyun \(n + 1\) ki power? Kyun ke general term \(a_k = a\,r^{k-1}\) hai, aur \(k = n + 2\) rakhne se power \(n + 1\) banti hai. Is equation se pehle \(r\) nikaalein, phir \(G_1 = ar,\ G_2 = ar^{2}\) wagaira. Agle hisse ki Example 17 bilkul isi tareeqe se hal hogi.

blocks.title: Hamari taraf se misaal
blocks.text:
\(2\) aur \(54\) ke beech do real G.M.s daaliye. G.P.: \(2, G_1, G_2, 54\), kul 4 terms, to \(54 = 2r^{3}\).
\[r^{3} = 27 \Rightarrow r = 3\]
\(G_1 = 2 \times 3 = 6\), \(G_2 = 2 \times 9 = 18\). Tasdeeq: \(2, 6, 18, 54\) mein har term pichli ka teen guna hai. Sahi!

blocks.title: Khud sochiye
blocks.text:
1. \(3\) aur \(27\) ka positive G.M. kya hai? (Ishara: \(3 \times 27 = 81\).)
2. Kya \(-2\) aur \(-8\) ka G.M. real hoga? \(ab\) ka sign dekh kar faisla kijiye.
3. \(a\) aur \(b\) ke beech 3 G.M.s daalne hon to \(b\) G.P. ki kaunsi term hogi?

blocks.title: Yaad rakhne wali baatein
blocks.text:
1. \(a, G, b\) G.P. mein hon to \(G\) geometric mean hai.
2. \(\frac{G}{a} = \frac{b}{G}\), is liye \(G^{2} = ab\) aur \(G = \pm\sqrt{ab}\).
3. Dono numbers positive hon to do real G.M.s; 'positive G.M.' \(\sqrt{ab}\) hai.
4. Signs ulte hon to G.M. imaginary (complex) hota hai.
5. \(n\) G.M.s daalne se G.P. ki kul \(n + 2\) terms banti hain, aur \(b = ar^{n+1}\).

blocks.title: Aam ghaltiyan
blocks.text:
1. G.M. ke liye \(\frac{a+b}{2}\) likh dena: yeh A.M. hai. G.M. mein zarb aur square root aata hai.
2. \(\pm\) bhool jana: \(4, -6, 9\) bhi G.P. hai, sirf \(4, 6, 9\) nahin.
3. Terms ginne mein ghalti: \(n\) G.M.s daalne par aakhri term \(n\)th nahin balke \((n+2)\)th hoti hai; is liye power \(n + 1\) aati hai.
4. \(\sqrt{ab}\) ko \(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}\) samajh lena: \(\sqrt{4 \times 9} = 6\), jab ke \(\sqrt{4} + \sqrt{9} = 5\).
